content: 1. The appropriate and timely utilization of health services, accurate diagnosis, and prompt reporting of dengue cases are critical. Acceptance of dengue vaccination, once recommended, is also essential for effective disease control. 2. The World Health Organization (WHO) must advocate for specific behavioral outcomes among its partners and Member States. This includes incorporating communication strategies into all relevant documents addressing dengue and vector-borne diseases. 3. Effective communication during outbreak responses is vital. It should promote specific, measurable, appropriate, realistic, and time-bound (SMART) behaviors for outbreak prevention and control. This ensures that interventions are implemented effectively and resources, such as personnel, funds, and supplies, are allocated efficiently to enable rapid and appropriate responses. 4. Data from multiple sources must be collected and analyzed to assess the event, evaluate the effectiveness of interventions, and determine the technical inputs required to control the outbreak. 5. Teams must engage with healthcare workers, patients, public health officials, NGOs, and response partners to quickly assess the situation and implement appropriate control and prevention measures. 6. Risk communication strategies must be developed and implemented to prepare national systems, stakeholders, and partners for effective responses to outbreaks. 7. Behavioral and social interventions should be designed and implemented to prepare communities for public health measures and promote risk reduction. 8. Training of staff at national and regional levels must be coordinated, and an inventory of expertise should be maintained for use when needed. 9. Capacity-building efforts for dengue prevention and control have been neglected. Training programs are often not sustained or scaled up to the national level, which hinders the effective implementation of global strategies. 10. Adequate staffing, access to appropriate equipment and facilities, and the necessary knowledge, competencies, and skills are required to execute, monitor, and evaluate dengue control programs effectively. 11. Program management must be strengthened to ensure sustainable dengue prevention and control. Collaboration among social scientists, communication specialists, public health entomologists, vector control personnel, epidemiologists, diagnostic laboratory staff, and healthcare professionals is essential. 12. Training activities should be tailored to the needs of various personnel groups, integrate adult learning techniques, and focus on improving the performance of multidisciplinary teams. 13. WHO has published guidance on various components of dengue control programs, including diagnosis, case management, prevention, control, and communication strategies. These documents must be adapted to local needs and widely disseminated to benefit stakeholders and avoid duplication of efforts. 14. Local health systems are increasingly responsible for a wide range of disease prevention and control activities. However, they are often unprepared for managing dengue outbreaks due to insufficient resources (human, technical, and financial). 15. Simulation exercises should be developed by WHO for use at the local level to maintain response management expertise during long inter-epidemic periods. 16. Managers require support from their superiors to ensure that dengue prevention and control activities receive adequate attention within broader communicable disease control programs. 17. Decision-makers, planners, and program managers must prioritize control and outbreak measures while safeguarding against potential changes in disease epidemiology. Access to a panel of technical experts is necessary to inform decision-making. 18. Sustainability and continuity of control measures are crucial. A participatory approach at the local level is needed, with key decision-makers forging partnerships with community leaders to enhance communication and collaboration. 19. Existing networks for responding to public health emergencies, extending from government to community levels, should be recognized and utilized whenever possible. 20. Local health services should integrate key components such as surveillance, entomology, environmental management, communication, and laboratory services for better decision-making and efficient resource use. 21. National regulations on vector control or pesticides may need to be adapted to integrate surveillance and control measures as mandatory contributions from local authorities, including community leaders, to the national plan. 22. A functional monitoring and evaluation system is essential for the successful implementation of the dengue strategy. It guides planning and implementation, assesses effectiveness, identifies areas for improvement, and optimizes resource use. 23. Monitoring and evaluation are weak links in most dengue programs and require urgent strengthening and integration. Relevant training programs are available at national and international levels. 24. Combining monitoring and evaluation allows for identifying successes and shortcomings, from which lessons can be learned to inform decision-making. 25. Indicators for resource use, processes, behavior, epidemiology, and entomology must be developed at decentralized levels of the health system. A single national system for collecting, analyzing, interpreting, and using monitoring and evaluation data is encouraged to reduce the reporting burden. 26. WHO collects a minimum set of dengue indicators from Member States, including suspected cases, confirmed cases, severe dengue cases, and deaths. Standardization of indicators is necessary for the global strategy. 27. Accurate surveillance should be the ultimate goal for dengue programs, as it provides the best assessment of disease burden and trends. Routine surveillance offers advantages for estimating case incidence spatially and temporally. 28. Data compiled annually allows for understanding the effects of various factors influencing dengue outbreaks and prevalence, such as climatic variation, serotype changes, and control interventions. 29. Monitoring and evaluation are critical components of dengue surveillance programs, systems that provide guidance and risk assessment, and outbreak response plans. These should include vector thresholds, virus prevalence, and incidence rates.
